title: JESUS KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM… SO WHY DID HE CHOOSE HIM ANYWAY?
paragraphs: JESUS KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM… SO WHY DID HE CHOOSE HIM ANYWAY?

He gave Judas a place among the Twelve, trusted him with a ministry, washed his feet, and shared a final meal with him. Jesus knew how the story would end. But the most terrifying part of Judas's story isn't what he did to Jesus. It's what his story might reveal about us.
There is something deeply unsettling about the way Jesus chose His disciples.
He knew.
Before Judas ever kissed Him in the garden, Jesus knew.
Before thirty pieces of silver changed hands, Jesus knew.

Before the religious leaders plotted His arrest, before the torches pierced the darkness of Gethsemane, before the betrayal became public, Jesus already knew the heart of the man who would hand Him over.
And still…
He chose Judas.
Not as a distant follower who occasionally listened to His sermons.
Not as a stranger standing somewhere in the crowd.
But as one of the Twelve.

Judas heard the teachings that changed history. He witnessed miracles that defied human explanation. He traveled with the Son of God. He shared meals with the One who would become the Bread of Life for a starving world.
And when Jesus sent the Twelve out to preach, Judas was included.
Think about that.
The man who would betray Jesus was first entrusted with representing Him.
Why?
Why would the all-knowing Son of God deliberately choose someone He knew would eventually betray Him?
Was Judas simply born to be a villain?
Was he trapped in a story he could never change?
Did Jesus need someone to betray Him so the cross could happen?
Or is there something far more disturbing—and far more revealing—hidden inside this question?
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Judas is not that he walked away from Jesus.
Perhaps it is that he walked so closely with Jesus while his heart was moving somewhere else.
And if that is possible…
Then this story is not merely about Judas.
It is about every person who has ever mistaken being near Jesus for truly belonging to Him.
The betrayal did not begin with a kiss.
It began long before the garden.
John 6 takes us into one of the most painful moments in Jesus' earthly ministry.
Jesus had been teaching difficult truths about Himself as the Bread of Life. Many who had followed Him could not accept what He was saying.
They had seen His power.
They had enjoyed His provision.
But when His words confronted their expectations, their enthusiasm began to collapse.
John 6:66 records:
"From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him." (KJV)
Imagine the scene.
People leaving.
Footsteps fading.
Faces that once looked toward Jesus with excitement now turning away.
And Jesus did not chase them with a watered-down message.
Instead, He turned toward the Twelve and asked:
"Will ye also go away?" (John 6:67, KJV)
Peter answered with one of the most beautiful confessions in Scripture:
"Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." (John 6:68, KJV)
But then Jesus said something that should make every reader stop.
"Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" (John 6:70, KJV)
John immediately explains that Jesus was speaking about Judas Iscariot, who would betray Him.
Here is the detail we must not overlook.
Jesus did not discover Judas's betrayal at the Last Supper.
He was not surprised in Gethsemane.
John 6:64 explicitly tells us:
"For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him." (KJV)
The Greek text uses the expression:
ᾔδει γὰρ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Ēdei gar ex archēs ho Iēsous.
"For Jesus knew from the beginning."
The verb ᾔδει (ēdei) expresses knowledge. John is not portraying Jesus as someone gradually piecing together suspicious behavior.
Jesus knew.
Yet we need to be careful with what this passage actually says.

The words "from the beginning" establish Jesus' prior knowledge in the context of John's narrative. They do not, by themselves, explain every philosophical question about divine foreknowledge, human freedom, or predestination.
And when Jesus called one of the Twelve "a devil," the Greek word was διάβολός (diabolos), meaning a slanderer or adversary, and often used for the devil.
Jesus was exposing the terrible spiritual opposition represented by Judas. He was not saying Judas was literally Satan himself.
This distinction matters.
Because if we are going to understand Judas, we must resist the temptation to turn Scripture into something more dramatic than what God actually revealed.
The truth is already powerful enough.
Jesus knowingly chose a man who would betray Him.
And the Gospel writers want us to wrestle with that reality.
But why choose him?
The first answer is that Judas's betrayal did not overthrow God's plan of redemption.
It unfolded within a story God already knew.
Jesus said in John 13:18:
"...that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me." (KJV)
Jesus was referring to Psalm 41:9, where David lamented betrayal by a trusted companion.
In its original setting, the psalm describes the anguish of someone betrayed by a person who had shared his bread.
In Jesus, that ancient pattern of intimate betrayal finds a profound fulfillment.
The Greek expression in John 13:18 is:
ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ
Hina hē graphē plērōthē.
"So that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
But listen carefully.
Fulfillment does not mean that Judas was innocent of his decision.
Scripture never treats his betrayal as morally harmless simply because God knew it would happen.
Jesus Himself declared:
"The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed!" (Matthew 26:24, KJV)
Both truths stand together.
God's redemptive purpose would be accomplished.
Judas remained responsible for his betrayal.
Acts 2:23 describes Jesus as delivered up according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, while also holding those responsible for His crucifixion accountable.
God's sovereignty does not turn evil into goodness.
Nor does God's foreknowledge make betrayal an act of obedience.
The Bible does not give us a complete philosophical explanation of how divine sovereignty and human responsibility fit together.
It does insist that both are real.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because knowing the truth about Jesus does not automatically mean our hearts have surrendered to Him.
Judas knew things about Jesus that many people today would give anything to have witnessed.
He heard His voice without a microphone.
He saw His face without a painting.
He walked the roads of Galilee beside Him.
And yet proximity to holiness did not produce a holy heart.
That is terrifying.
You can attend church every Sunday and still be spiritually distant.
You can memorize Bible verses while secretly negotiating with sin.
You can sing about surrender while refusing to surrender the one thing God keeps confronting.
You can defend Christianity in public while resisting Christ in private.
You can even participate in ministry and mistake usefulness for intimacy with God.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:21–23 that not everyone who calls Him Lord, or even claims remarkable works in His name, truly belongs to Him.
That warning is not meant to make sincere believers despair every time they struggle.
It is meant to expose the deadly danger of a faith that knows religious language but refuses the Lordship of Christ.
And Judas stands before us as one of Scripture's most sobering examples.
He was close enough to hear the heartbeat of the ministry, but his own heart was not surrendered to the Messiah.
There is another detail that makes this story even more heartbreaking.
Judas was entrusted with the money bag.
John 12:6 identifies him as the keeper of the common funds and says he stole from them.
Think about the contrast.
Jesus was teaching people to treasure what lasts forever.
Judas was secretly taking what would eventually perish.
Jesus was giving Himself away.
Judas was taking for himself.
Jesus was moving toward the cross.
Judas was moving toward a transaction.
And when Mary anointed Jesus with costly perfume, Judas objected that it could have been sold and the money given to the poor.
His words sounded compassionate.
But John exposes the motive behind them.
It was not concern for the poor.
It was greed.
This is one of the most dangerous ways sin operates.
It learns to speak the language of righteousness.
Greed can disguise itself as stewardship.
Pride can disguise itself as spiritual maturity.
Bitterness can disguise itself as discernment.
Control can disguise itself as leadership.
And sometimes the sin we refuse to confront becomes so familiar that we stop recognizing it.
We begin defending what we should be confessing.
Judas's story should make us ask an uncomfortable question:
What have I become skilled at justifying?
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is the dishonesty you keep calling necessary.
Maybe it is the private addiction hidden behind your public reputation.
Maybe it is the resentment you have carried for years while insisting you have forgiven.
Maybe it is your obsession with money, recognition, approval, or control.
The danger is not that every struggle makes you Judas.
It does not.
The danger is allowing sin to remain unchallenged until the voice of conviction becomes easier to ignore.
Judas did not simply make one isolated mistake.
The Gospel accounts show a developing pattern of unbelief, dishonesty, greed, and ultimately betrayal.
And yet, even knowing what Judas would do, Jesus continued toward the cross.
Then came the night when Jesus knelt before the feet of His betrayer.
John 13 describes a scene so astonishing that familiarity can rob it of its force.
The disciples were gathered for supper.
Jesus knew His hour had come.
He knew where He had come from.
He knew where He was going.
And He knew the betrayal that was approaching.
Then He rose from supper, laid aside His outer garments, took a towel, and began washing His disciples' feet.
The Lord of glory performed the work of a servant.
The One through whom all things were made knelt before men made from dust.
And Judas was among them.
John does not separately narrate the exact moment Jesus washed Judas's feet, but the passage presents the washing of the disciples before Judas's departure, with no exception stated.
The natural reading is that Judas was included.
Do you understand the weight of that?
Jesus knew what Judas would do.
And still He stooped.
He did not wash the feet of the innocent.
There were no innocent men in that room.
He washed the feet of men who would soon fail Him in different ways.
Peter would deny Him.
The others would scatter.
And Judas would betray Him.
Yet the Son of God took the posture of a servant.
This was not weakness.
This was the extraordinary humility of Christ.
John 13:1 says that Jesus loved His own "unto the end."
The Greek expression is:
εἰς τέλος
Eis telos.
It can convey love to the end, or love to the fullest extent, depending on the nuance understood in context.
John is showing us the steadfast character of Jesus' love.
But we must not distort that love into the idea that repentance is unnecessary or that betrayal has no consequences.
Jesus' humility does not erase Judas's responsibility.
His love is not permission to continue in darkness.
It is a revelation of the Savior's character—a character so different from ours that it should bring us to our knees.
Because most of us struggle to show kindness to someone who has merely spoken badly about us.
Jesus served in the presence of the man who would deliver Him to His enemies.
And now the question is no longer simply, "Why did Jesus choose Judas?"
It becomes:
"What kind of Savior is this?"
What kind of King lays aside His garments to serve?
What kind of Lord knows betrayal is coming and still refuses to abandon His mission?
What kind of love walks toward suffering with eyes fully open?
The answer is Jesus Christ.
Not a sentimental version of Him.
Not a Savior invented to affirm everything we want.
The real Jesus.
Holy.
Righteous.
Humble.
Truthful.
Merciful.
And utterly committed to accomplishing the Father's will.
Then came the bread.
During the supper, Jesus identified His betrayer by giving him a morsel.
John 13:26–27 records the moment.
After Judas received the morsel, Satan entered into him, and Jesus told him to do quickly what he was going to do.
There is no need to invent a hidden conversation or imagine expressions Scripture never describes.
The text itself is devastating.
Judas had shared the table.
He had received the morsel.
And he went out.
Then John adds four words that seem almost unbearable:
"And it was night." (John 13:30, KJV)
Night.
A literal detail of the setting.
But in a Gospel where light and darkness carry profound theological meaning, it also resonates with the spiritual darkness of the betrayal.
The man who had walked with the Light of the world stepped out into the night.
And this is where we should stop pretending that every spiritual tragedy begins with someone openly rejecting God.
Sometimes the most dangerous departure happens quietly.
No announcement.
No public argument.
No dramatic renunciation.
Just a heart that has been drifting for so long that eventually the feet follow.
Someone stops praying honestly.
Then stops listening.
Then stops confessing.
Then starts defending what they once resisted.
And one day, the things that once brought conviction barely trouble them anymore.

Not every season of spiritual dryness is rebellion. Not every exhausted believer is hardening their heart. Some people are wounded, grieving, overwhelmed, or struggling under burdens others cannot see.
Jesus is compassionate toward the weary.
But deliberate, cherished sin is different from a believer crying out for help in weakness.
Judas's story warns us not to confuse those two things.
If you are fighting sin, grieving your failures, and longing to return to Christ, do not read Judas's story as proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
Hear the invitation of the Gospel.
Come into the light.
Confess what you have hidden.
Do not wait until your heart feels worthy.
You cannot make yourself worthy of grace.
That is why you need a Savior.
And then came the kiss.
Matthew 26:48–50 describes Judas identifying Jesus to the arresting crowd with a kiss.
A gesture normally associated with affection became the signal of betrayal.
And Jesus addressed him as "Friend" in Matthew 26:50.
The Greek word is ἑταῖρε (hetaire), a form of address meaning companion or friend.

It should not be exaggerated into a claim that the word necessarily expressed intimate affection or guaranteed an offer of forgiveness at that exact moment. Jesus also uses this form of address in other settings, including rebuke.
Still, the scene is staggering.
The betrayer approaches.
The arresting crowd waits.
The kiss is given.
And Jesus does not lose control of the situation.
In John 10:18, Jesus had already declared that no one took His life from Him against His will. He laid it down of His own accord.
Judas's betrayal was real.
The religious leaders' hostility was real.
The injustice of the trial and crucifixion was real.
But Jesus was not a helpless victim of circumstances beyond God's control.
He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
The cross was not merely the consequence of Judas's betrayal.
It was the place where the sinless Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved, fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (KJV)
And 1 Peter 2:24 says Christ bore our sins in His own body on the tree.
Jesus did not die because God needed evil people to defeat Him.
Jesus died because He came to save sinners.
Judas's evil did not become righteous because God accomplished redemption through the events surrounding the cross.
Instead, God demonstrated His power and wisdom by accomplishing His saving purpose even through the wicked actions of human beings.
What people intended for evil did not defeat the purpose of God.
And on the third day, the crucified Christ rose from the dead.
That is why our hope is not ultimately found in understanding every mystery about Judas.
Our hope is found in the risen Jesus.
But the story takes an even more painful turn.
Judas regretted what he had done.

Matthew 27:3–5 tells us that when Judas saw Jesus condemned, he was seized with remorse, returned the thirty pieces of silver, confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood, and then went away and hanged himself.
The Greek verb used for Judas's remorse is μεταμεληθείς (metamelētheis).
It expresses regret or a change of feeling about what one has done.
The New Testament also uses μετάνοια (metanoia) and related words for repentance, often emphasizing a turning of mind and life toward God.
We must be precise here.

The distinction between these Greek word families is not an absolute rule that one always means shallow regret and the other always means genuine repentance. Their meanings overlap, and context matters.
In Judas's case, Matthew records real remorse and a confession of wrongdoing, but not a return to Jesus in trusting faith.
His story ends in tragedy.
And Scripture does not invite us to speculate about every unrecorded thought that passed through his mind.
It gives us enough to recognize the horror of sin and the seriousness of betrayal.
But then consider Peter.
Peter also failed Jesus.
Not by selling Him for silver, but by denying that he knew Him.
Three times.
The disciple who had boldly declared his loyalty collapsed under fear.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered Jesus' words and wept bitterly.
Two men.
Two devastating failures.
Two stories involving men who had lived close to Jesus.
Yet their recorded endings are profoundly different.
Judas's story moves toward despair and death.
Peter's story moves toward restoration.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter and restored him to service in John 21.
The difference is not that Peter's sin was insignificant.
It was not.
Nor should we claim to know every hidden motive that distinguished these two men.
But Scripture clearly shows Peter being brought back into fellowship and service through the risen Christ.
And that is where grace becomes more than a beautiful religious word.
Grace is what you need when you cannot undo what you have done.
Grace is what you need when your promises have collapsed.
Grace is what you need when you discover that your courage was smaller than you imagined.
Grace is what you need when the person you thought you were has been exposed by the choices you made.
Peter could not travel backward and erase his denials.
But Jesus was not finished with Peter.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else.
You cannot undo yesterday.
You cannot retrieve every word spoken in anger.
You cannot erase every secret decision.
You cannot recover every wasted opportunity.
But if you are alive today, the call to repent and believe in Jesus Christ still confronts you.
Do not confuse conviction with a sentence that says you are beyond mercy.
Conviction can be the very thing that drives you to the Savior.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
The promise rests on God's faithfulness and the saving work of Jesus Christ, not on our ability to manufacture perfect emotions.
You do not have to pretend your sin was small.
You need to come to the One whose grace is sufficient to forgive sinners who repent and trust in Him.
And if your failures have left you feeling trapped in despair, do not isolate yourself. Reach out to a trusted person, pastor, or qualified counselor who can walk with you toward safety and hope.
Your life is not beyond the reach of help.
Now return to the original question.
Why did Jesus choose Judas when He knew Judas would betray Him?
Scripture gives us several truths that belong together.
Jesus knowingly chose Judas as one of the Twelve.
Judas's betrayal fulfilled Scripture and did not derail God's redemptive purpose.
Judas was morally responsible for his actions.
Jesus exposed the danger of unbelief concealed beneath outward discipleship.
And through everything, Jesus revealed that His journey to the cross was neither accidental nor beyond His knowledge.
But Scripture does not tell us every reason God permitted Judas to occupy that particular place.
We should not pretend it does.
The Bible does not say Judas was created solely to betray Jesus.
It does not say Judas was forced to sin against his will.
It does not teach that his betrayal was a righteous act because it contributed to events leading to the crucifixion.
And it does not authorize us to conclude that every person who struggles spiritually is another Judas.
What it does show us is a Savior who knew the darkness He would face and still willingly went to the cross.
A Savior who did not need to discover humanity's sinfulness before deciding whether sinners were worth saving.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we learned to hide our brokenness more convincingly.
While we were still sinners.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that God ignores evil.
Not that holiness no longer matters.
Not that repentance can be replaced with religious emotion.
But that the holy God has made a way for guilty people to be forgiven and reconciled to Him through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
That is not a slogan meant to make sin sound romantic.
Sin destroys.
Betrayal wounds.
Greed corrupts.
Unbelief hardens.
And Judas's story ends with a tragedy that should never be trivialized.
But the Gospel announces something greater than the power of sin.
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
The cross declares the seriousness of our guilt.
The empty tomb declares the triumph of our Savior.
And the invitation to repent and believe means that your past does not have to be the final authority over your future.
So before you close this article, I want to ask you something.
Not about Judas.
About you.
Are you following Jesus because you love Him, or only because you love what you hope He will give you?
Are you willing to obey Him when His words challenge the life you have built?
Is there something you keep hidden because you are afraid of what surrender might cost?
Have you been wearing the appearance of faith while slowly drifting away from its Author?
Or are you a weary believer who has mistaken your struggle for proof that Christ no longer wants you?
Whatever your answer, do not respond by putting on another religious performance.
Come honestly before God.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
And the One who knows is the One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His Son.
You may pray:

"Lord Jesus, You know what I have hidden. You know the sins I have excused, the promises I have broken, and the ways I have resisted Your truth. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Turn my heart away from sin and toward You. Teach me to follow You sincerely, not merely appear close to You. Where I have grown cold, awaken me. Where I have become proud, humble me. Where I have fallen, lead me into repentance and restoration. Let my life belong to You. Amen."
And if this story exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private struggle.
Not because a comment earns God's attention.
Not because public words prove salvation.
But because sometimes one honest confession of need opens the door to encouragement, prayer, and fellowship.
And someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only person struggling.
Not merely because a page needs reach.
But because somewhere among your friends and family there may be someone who looks spiritually fine while quietly drifting away.
Someone who believes their failure is too great for forgiveness.
Someone who needs to hear the difference between religious appearance and genuine surrender.
Someone who has almost given up on returning to Christ.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have walked away from church to follow along.
There is room here for serious questions, honest struggles, and a deeper search for biblical truth.
And if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter the Gospel, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not pressured or compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You glorify Him through faith in Christ and a life shaped by His grace and truth.
It can help sustain the time, effort, and resources required to prepare biblical content, encourage readers, and reach people beyond our existing community.
The greater invitation is to become part of a community that values biblical nourishment, accountability, encouragement, and a deeper walk with Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
And God's grace cannot be purchased.

Our hope is simply that those who have been strengthened through this ministry, and who are financially able, will consider helping us continue bringing Scripture-centered encouragement to more people.
Even a thoughtful share may introduce someone to a biblical truth they have never seriously considered.
And that brings us back to Judas.
A man who walked beside Jesus.
A man who heard His words.
A man who witnessed His works.
A man who was chosen as an apostle and still betrayed Him.
His story warns us that outward nearness to sacred things cannot replace a heart surrendered to God.
But Peter's restoration reminds us that failure does not have to be the final chapter for those who return to Christ.
And the cross tells us why.
Jesus knew the cost of redemption.
He knew the betrayal.
He knew the suffering.
He knew the cross.
And He willingly gave Himself to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.
So do not end this story merely asking why Jesus chose Judas.
Ask whether you are truly trusting Jesus.
Not just admiring Him.
Not just speaking about Him.
Not just being associated with people who follow Him.
But turning from sin and trusting the crucified and risen Lord.
Because in the end, the most important question is not how close Judas stood to Jesus.
It is whether your heart has surrendered to the Savior who still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Judas reminds us that you can stand close enough to kiss Jesus and still refuse to surrender your heart; the cross reminds us that no sinner who truly comes to Christ needs to remain in the darkness.
